chunks: How a flip-flop or latch works. The question: How does a flip flop/latch work?
A flip-flop or latch remembers one bit by feeding a circuit's output back into its own input. Two cross-coupled gates settle into one of two stable states, 0 or 1, and stay there.
Add an enable and you get a D latch. Put two latches in series with opposite enables and you get a flip-flop that changes only at a clock edge.
Think of a rocker light switch. Push it up and it stays up; push it down and it stays down. It remembers which way it was last pushed.
Balanced exactly in the middle, it is unstable, and the slightest nudge tips it one way or the other. A gate loop does the same: feedback reinforces whichever state it is in.
The solid curve is one inverter's transfer function; the dashed curve is the other inverter's, drawn with axes swapped.

They intersect at three points: two full-rail states that are stable (the slope product is less than one there, so errors shrink) and one at the switching threshold, which is unstable (slope product greater than one, so errors grow).
Positive feedback: feeding an output back so that it reinforces its own state, giving two stable states (bistable).
NOR gate: a logic gate whose output is 1 only when both inputs are 0. Cross-coupled means each gate's output feeds the other's input.
SR latch: two cross-coupled NOR gates with set (S) and reset (R) inputs. D latch: a gated latch whose output follows input D while its enable is active.
Master-slave: two latches with opposite enables, forming a flip-flop.
Take an SR latch made of two cross-coupled NOR gates. Say it stores Q = 1. With S and R both 0, it just holds. Pulse R to 1. The top NOR now outputs 0, so Q = 0.
That makes the other output 1, and the loop locks in the new state. Return R to 0 and Q stays 0. Pulsing S to 1 does the reverse.
Setting S and R both to 1 is forbidden, because both outputs go to 0 and releasing them together is unpredictable.
"Feedback is the key. Two cross-coupled NOR gates form an SR latch with two stable states, so it stores a bit: set, reset, or hold, with both inputs high forbidden.
Gate the inputs with an enable and tie them to D and its complement and you get a D latch, which is transparent while enabled.

Put two D latches in series with opposite enables and you get a flip-flop: the master captures D while the clock is low, and at the rising edge the slave takes it to Q, so the output only changes on the edge."
